Packaging & Delivery Service Senior Assistant
About the role
You will join the Bodleian Libraries’ Packaging and Delivery Service (PADS), helping to protect and transport important library, archive and museum collections. The service provides specialist packaging, collection moves and preventative conservation support across Oxford and beyond.
You will make and fit protective boxes and folders, operate specialist equipment and software, process orders, and respond to customer enquiries. Working with colleagues, you will plan safe collection moves, maintain accurate records and support deliveries at University sites and occasionally elsewhere in the UK.
The work includes regular manual handling and some working at height.
This is a full-time post, working 36.5 hours per week.
About You
You will have strong organisational, problem-solving and communication skills, with excellent attention to detail and accurate numeracy and data entry.
You will be confident working independently and collaboratively, balancing competing deadlines and responding to enquiries.
You will be comfortable using machinery and undertaking careful manual handling, proficient in Microsoft Office and willing to learn specialist software.
Experience in logistics, libraries or museums, knowledge of preventative conservation or a UK driving licence would be advantageous.

We are looking for  a People and Culture Coordinator join the National Theatre's People and Culture team.

title: Assistant Professor in Corporate Law  1 year  (Fixed Term)
description:
The Faculty of Law is seeking to appoint an appropriately qualified individual to an Assistant Professorship in Corporate Law from 1 October 2027.
The person appointed will be expected to teach at undergraduate and postgraduate levels on corporate law papers, to conduct research and participate in the general work of the Faculty.
Whilst it is unlikely that the postholder would be expected to take on any supervision of PhD students due to the length of the appointment, the postholder may be invited to contribute to our research training programme.
Assistant Professors are also expected to examine, and from time to time, to serve on Faculty committees and undertake other administrative responsibilities.
The person appointed will:
be an outstanding scholar of Corporate Law
teach on the Faculty's corporate law courses including Deals on the MCL, Corporate  Governance on the LLM and Tripos (i.e. undergraduate) Company Law
demonstrate potential to lecture effectively and to publish research of the highest calibre
hold a Master's Degree, or a PhD equivalent qualification
The Faculty is one of the worlds leading law schools. It is consistently ranked highly in the United Kingdom, in national league tables, and in the QS World University Rankings. The Faculty of Law currently has over 100 University, Faculty and College teaching officers. Almost every area of legal interest is represented.
The Faculty of Law successfully renewed its Athena Swan Bronze Award in January 2026. This recognition highlights our ongoing efforts to advance gender equality and build an inclusive culture across the institution.
We expect to be able to notify applicants whether they have been shortlisted by Tuesday 12 January 2027. Interviews, which will involve giving a short presentation, will take place in-person in Cambridge on Tuesday 19 January 2027.

title: Deputy Biofacility Manager
description:
We are looking to recruit an experienced and motivated Deputy Biofacility Manager to be part of a hardworking team in a busy biomedical facility situated in Cambridge.
You will assist the Biofacility manager with the day to day management of the biofacility and deputise in their absence. You will coordinate the animal husbandry work of the facility, supervising a team of technicians, coordinating the activity and staffing allocations of the team to ensure the smooth day-to-day running of the facility and maintain high standards of animal care and welfare. You will assist the Biofacility Manager with the recruitment, training and assessment of new staff with in-house policies and procedures as well as working to Home Office regulations and performance management. You will undertake both licenced and unlicensed scientific procedures along with daily husbandry and maintenance to assist the technicians as required. You are responsible for the maintenance of all necessary records, referring any issues and concerns to the Biofacility Manager as necessary.
You will be able to work both independently and as part of a team, with experience supervising or managing staff. You will have IAT Level 3 or equivalent, Home Office Licence modules A ¿ C and will be a Personal Licence holder. In depth experience of working within a biofacility with IVCs is essential, as are excellent communication skills. You must be able to use a computerised data management system and have previous experience working in a supervisory / team leader role. Knowledge of relevant Home Office, and Health and Safety legislation is important, as is knowledge and experience in the principals of aseptic surgery and specialised breeding techniques.

About us
King’s College London is a world-leading university based in the heart of London. The Faculty of Natural, Mathematical & Engineering Sciences brings together research and education in mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science and engineering, with a strong emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration, innovation and addressing fundamental scientific questions and wider societal challenges.
The Department of Mathematics, based at the University’s Strand Campus in central London, has a long and distinguished tradition in pure and applied mathematics, dating back to 1830. Today, the Department is a leading centre for mathematics research in the UK, fostering a vibrant, international and collaborative research environment. Its research spans a broad range of areas, including analysis, disordered systems, financial mathematics, geometry, number theory, probability, statistics and theoretical physics, with strong connections across King’s and with external academic and industrial partners.
The Theoretical Physics Group in the Department of Mathematics is at the international forefront of research in string and M-theory, black holes, conformal field theory, supersymmetry, integrability, and other fundamental branches of modern theoretical physics. The group has a highly interactive research culture with multiple weekly activities including seminars, journal clubs and lecture series. title: Marie Sklodowska-Curie Early Stage Researchers - A systematic data assimilation model to predict thermoacoustic instabilities
description:
This studentship is one of 15 across Europe in the Marie Curie ITN HyNOISE (
https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101311721
)
The overall objective is to optimize the design of hydrogen-fuelled gas turbine injectors, so that combustors are quiet and not susceptible to thermoacoustic instabilities. This requires a quantitatively-accurate model of the thermoacoustic behaviour of the combustor. This model will be obtained by data assimilation from laboratory experiments (NTNU), large eddy simulations (TUB), and industrial experiments. This data will be assimilated into thermoacoustic models using UCAM's adjoint-accelerated inference and optimization method (AXIOM).
The first intermediate objective is to extend AXIOM to typical hydrogen flame geometries using data from a laboratory scale combustor at NTNU with Bayesian model selection. The second intermediate objective is to extend AXIOM to industrial scale geometries using data from a real gas turbine fuel injector on an industrial test rig. Bayesian experimental design will be used to identify the experimental configurations that maximize the information that can be learned from a limited number of tests. The third intermediate objective is to develop and test several candidate mean field flame models with TUB and then to assimilate LES data into these models with AXIOM. The result will be a Bayesian framework that transfers data from experiments and numerical simulations into low order models. These models will steadily accumulate data and become more accurate over time. They can therefore be used for optimization and re-optimization, as more data become available in the future.
Research Objectives
-Assimilation of experimental data from a laboratory scale combustor into thermoacoustic models and flame models. 
-Assimilation of experimental data from an industrial scale test rig into thermoacoustic models. 
-Development and testing of several candidate mean field flame models with TUB.

title: Research Assistant/Associate in Power Electronics Packaging and Integration in Power Electronics Packaging and Integration (Fixed Term)
description:
A position exists for a Research Assistant/Associate in Power Electronics Packaging and Integration in the Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, working with Professor Teng Long's Power Electronics Research Group in West Cambridge, UK.
The post holder will design and validate advanced chip-scale and module-level packages for SiC and GaN devices, including die attachment, interconnections, thermal interfaces and heat-spreading structures. Research will combine electrical, thermal and thermomechanical modelling with power semiconductor electrical and thermal testing. Duties include finite-element and compact thermal-network modelling, parameter extraction, transient thermal impedance measurements, structure-function analysis and junction-to-case thermal resistance assessment. Experimental results will validate models and guide improvements in package design. Power cycling and failure analysis will link package degradation to measured changes in device behaviour. The post holder will develop automated testing and analysis methods, publish findings, collaborate with academic and industrial partners, and contribute to student supervision and research proposals.
Applicants must have, or be close to obtaining, a PhD in Electrical Engineering or a related discipline, with research in power electronics packaging, integration or thermal management. Knowledge of power semiconductor packaging, interconnections, thermal management and reliability is essential, together with at least two accepted or published journal papers. Experience in multiphysics or thermal-network modelling, semiconductor testing, transient thermal characterisation, or test automation and data analysis using MATLAB, Python or equivalent tools is desirable.

title: PhD Studentship (Fixed Term)
description:
3-Year Doctoral Training Programme: Long-term impact of early management strategies across the lifecourse in Crohn's disease
Start date: April 2027
Fully funded studentship
Applications are invited for a
3-Year Doctoral Training Programme
that brings together researchers from across the University of Cambridge, with a focus on the Lifecourse impact of early disease control and management strategies in Crohn's disease. This studentship will provide training in social sciences, mixed methods research including surveys and face to face interviews, data analysis, psychosocial impact measurement including consideration of long-term quality of life measures in a common chronic gastrointestinal condition.
One student will be selected for admission to the University of Cambridge and will benefit from co-supervision, training, collaboration and access to world-class research infrastructure across partner institutions
.
Instructions for applying are given below
.
There has been increasing understanding over the last decade about the importance of early inflammatory control in Crohn's disease. In the PROFILE trial 386 patients newly-diagnosed with Crohn's disease in 40 UK hospitals were randomised to either 'step-up' treatment, requiring courses of steroids and gradual escalation in immunosuppressant and then infliximab to treat flares, or 'top-down' infliximab from diagnosis. Clinical outcomes were strikingly better with 'top-down' therapy at both one year,1 and after 5-years. (Noor et al. Lancet Gastro Hep 2024; Noor et al. Lancet Gastro Hep 2026)
As well as the clinical benefits, we have also shown that early and effective control of inflammation reduces direct costs and is beneficial (cost-effective) to healthcare services (Noor et al. JCC 2025). But whether this is reflected in better real-world, psychosocial outcomes for patients is unknown. title: Research Associate (Electronic Health Records Data Scientist)
description:
We wish to appoint a Research Associate to work on a national project with the TIMELY Team, in the Department of Psychiatry, University of Cambridge. The TIMELY Team is working to build clinically useful digital tools to predict mental health problems in children and young people and to support prevention pathways. This role will support a collaborative project to establish and develop the National Mental Health (MH) Translational Research Collaborative's Secure Data Environment (MH-TRC SDE), leading data standardisation.
The appointee will work with the University of Cambridge team (Dr Anna Moore, Rudolph Cardinal), and collaborators at NHS Merseyside (Dr Jim Hughes, Informatics), University of Liverpool, Swansea University, Arden and Greater East Midlands CSU, King's College London, the SDE Network and HDR UK. The role is funded by the NIHR.
The project is focused on developing data resources to support MH research. The Research Associate will contribute to the creation of a population-wide, multi-agency database called CADRE (Child and Adolescent Data REsource), which combines data drawn from healthcare, social care, education, and other services. CADRE is one of many MH SDEs that support MH research nationally; these SDEs require their raw data to be standardised to the OMOP Common Data Model. The Research Associate will support a high-level landscape review of OMOP use for MH data. They will adapt the CADRE standardisation approach to SDEs in Birmingham, Liverpool, and Manchester, as part of the effort to build a streamlined toolkit/guidelines to support OMOP standardisation for MH SDEs nationally. We are especially interested in integrating digital tools, including artificial intelligence, to the standardisation process. The role will also communicate to the MH research community about the importance of data standardisation and promote the MH SDE toolkit.

title: Research Associate - Prywes Group (Fixed Term)
description:
The Prywes Lab at the University of Cambridge Biochemistry department is seeking a postdoc with experience in protein engineering. Experience with high throughput sequencing, metabolic circuit manipulation, microbiology and in vitro enzymology is desirable.
The Prywes lab studies studies enzyme evolution, mechanism and engineering (visit our website, pryweslab.org). We have previously generated a map of the rubisco biochemical landscape (Prywes et al. Nature 2025). Current lab aims include expanding that landscape and studying enzyme mechanism through high-throughput data generation.
The project for this position will involve growth-coupled E. coli strains to study enzyme properties in high throughput. The project will involve Machine-Learning for protein design, mutant library generation and cloning, library selection by E. coli growth and high throughput sequencing and analysis. In vitro enzymology will also be required. The ideal candidate will possess expertise in two or more of these techniques and demonstrate a willingness to learn new methods and concepts. Moreover, a suitable candidate will have completed a PhD and demonstrated a high research impact and extensive experience. We are looking for individuals who can think independently and serve as a driving force for their research projects.

). The University of Cambridge offers a vibrant scientific community, access to cutting-edge research facilities, and numerous collaboration opportunities. In our group, we foster an inclusive, friendly, and supportive environment to help all trainees achieve their scientific and career goals. title: Research Assistant / Associate (Fixed Term)
description:
Prof Maura Malpetti is looking for an enthusiastic Post-Doctoral Research Associate or Pre-Doctoral Research Assistant to join her lab at the Cambridge University Department of Clinical Neurosciences. The post is part of our Cambridge-based program aiming to investigate inflammation in frontotemporal dementia and accelerate the development of treatments for dementia. To this end, we established a multi-centre study, the UK-wide Open Network for Frontotemporal dementia Innovation Research (ON-FIRE), which involves data collection from >50 sites across the UK.
As a project lead and coordinator of ON-FIRE, you will coordinate site initiation and recruitments, samples delivery, contracts, data sharing, optimization of workflows, and facilitate Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement activities. You will also contribute towards the smooth running of projects based in Cambridge, helping in recruitment, assessment data and blood collection supported by experienced scientists, clinicians and research nurses. You will drive the project, develop and deliver the study's research objectives and be well equipped to present developments and key findings to relevant stakeholders. Building upon the postholder's centrality in the delivery of ON-FIRE, project-based analytical work on study data can also form a core component of the position.
For this post, you will have an undergraduate and/or a PhD in neurosciences, psychology, biomedical science or related discipline. You will have knowledge of clinical research, related research methods and applications, and project management skills. Experience in patient recruitment in research studies of dementia or mental health disorders would be advantageous. You will collaborate within a balanced team with post-doctoral scientists, clinical fellows, research nurses and students to ensure efficient research activities across the team and center.

title: Smuts Visiting Research Fellowship (Fixed Term)
description:
The Smuts Management Committee invites applications for a non-renewable Smuts Visiting Research Fellowship in Commonwealth Studies, tenable for 9 months commencing from 1st October 2027.
The Smuts Memorial Fund usually elects one Smuts Visiting Research Fellow a year to come to Cambridge to carry out research for up to 9 months. These Fellowships are intended for mid- to senior career academics, of international calibre in an institutional position and who received their PhD at least five years prior to the application closing date.
Fellows may come from any nationality, but should be normally resident outside the United Kingdom, and a wide variety of disciplines in the social sciences, arts and humanities. They are expected to advance Commonwealth Studies in Cambridge mainly by pursuing research, but also by taking part in seminars and similar activities within the University. During the tenure of their Fellowship, Fellows are required to deliver at least one public lecture in Cambridge arranged in consultation with the Managers of the Smuts Memorial Fund.
Commonwealth Studies is defined here as research that is focused on past or present countries and/or issues pertaining to one or more parts of the Commonwealth. Fellows will have access, by agreement, to the holdings of Faculty and Departmental libraries, to the libraries of the Centres of African Studies and South Asian Studies and to the University Library, which houses the extensive collection of materials relating to the history of the British Empire and Commonwealth, formerly housed in the Royal Commonwealth Society Library in London.
The Managers expect that the person appointed would be intending to come to Cambridge to work on a project that builds on existing research for which a period of residence in Cambridge is demonstrably appropriate, although they would not rule out a new piece of work that is expected to be completed by the end of the 9-month tenure of the Fellowship.

King’s College London is a world-leading university based in the heart of London. title: Marie Sklodowska-Curie Early Stage Researchers - A systematic data assimilation model to predict thermoacoustic instabilities
description:
This studentship is one of 15 across Europe in the Marie Curie ITN HyNOISE (
https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101311721
)
The overall objective is to optimize the design of hydrogen-fuelled gas turbine injectors, so that combustors are quiet and not susceptible to thermoacoustic instabilities. This requires a quantitatively-accurate model of the thermoacoustic behaviour of the combustor. This model will be obtained by data assimilation from laboratory experiments (NTNU), large eddy simulations (TUB), and industrial experiments (RRD). This data will be assimilated into thermoacoustic models using UCAM's adjoint-accelerated inference and optimization method (AXIOM).
The first intermediate objective is to extend AXIOM to typical hydrogen flame geometries using data from a laboratory scale combustor at NTNU with Bayesian model selection. The second intermediate objective is to extend AXIOM to industrial scale geometries using data from a real gas turbine fuel injector on an industrial test rig at RRD. Bayesian experimental design will be used to identify the experimental configurations that maximize the information that can be learned from a limited number of tests. The third intermediate objective is to develop and test several candidate mean field flame models with TUB and then to assimilate LES data into these models with AXIOM. The result will be a Bayesian framework that transfers data from experiments and numerical simulations into low order models. These models will steadily accumulate data and become more accurate over time. They can therefore be used for optimization and re-optimization, as more data become available in the future.
Research Objectives
-Assimilation of experimental data from a laboratory scale combustor into thermoacoustic models and flame models.
-Assimilation of experimental data from a RRD industrial scale test rig into thermoacoustic models.

The Department of Mathematics has a long and distinguished tradition in pure and applied mathematics, dating back to the appointment of King’s first Professor of Mathematics in 1830. Its research spans a broad range of areas, including analysis, disordered systems, financial mathematics, geometry, number theory, probability, statistics and theoretical physics, with strong connections across King’s and with external academic and industrial partners.

title: Research Associate (Fixed Term)
location_text: Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience
description:
We are inviting applications for a Postdoctoral Scientist to join the Röper lab at the Department of Physiology, Development and Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge. We investigate the mechanisms and mechanics of organ formation during development, by studying two complementary model systems of tube morphogenesis, the formation of the salivary glands in the Drosophila embryo and the formation of the nephron tube in human renal organoids in culture. We are looking for skilled and enthusiastic individuals with expertise in in renal biology in both model systems, human renal organoids and the Drosophila renal system.
You will contribute to a project investigating the role of the nucleus and its linkage to the intracellular cytoskeleton, focussing on the LINC complex and interactors in both human renal organoids during tube morphogenesis and also in Drosophila in the Malpighian tubules and nephrocytes that make up the fly's renal system.
You will conduct this work, using a combination of advanced imaging, quantitative and genetics approaches, as part of a team of researchers that tackle related questions across our two models.
Candidates should have or be about to receive a PhD in Cell Biology or Developmental Biology. You should have extensive experience of Drosophila husbandry and genetics, be experienced in modeling human renal conditions in a Drosophila model,  have experience in immunofluorescence labelling, confocal imaging and quantitative analyses as well as organoid culture. Skills in coding using Python or Matlab environments are essential.
Appointment at Research Associate level is dependent on having a PhD; those without a PhD will be appointed at Research Assistant level. Those who have submitted but not yet received their PhD will be appointed at Research Assistant level, which will be amended to Research Associate once the PhD has been awarded.
Salary Scales are: Research Assistant: £33,662 - £36,320, Research Associate: £38,448 - £46,970.

title: Research Associate (Fixed Term)
description:
The Medical Research Council Mitochondrial Biology Unit (MRC MBU), University of Cambridge wishes to appoint a post-doctoral Research Associate to join the research group of Prof. Edmund Kunji at the MRC Mitochondrial Biology Unit.
A world-renowned centre for research, the MRC MBU is a vibrant community focused on the involvement of mitochondria and their dysfunction in an ever-increasing range of human diseases. Additional information can be found at
www.mrc-mbu.cam.ac.uk
.
The postholder will contribute to a collaborative project between Professors Daniel A Tennant (University of Birmingham, UK) and Edmund RS Kunji (University of Cambridge, UK), called "Targeting mitochondrial oxidative stress in SDHB-deficient cancers." Pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas (PPGL) are rare neuroendocrine tumours arising from chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla and sympathetic/parasympathetic paraganglia, respectively. Approximately 40% of patients carry germline mutations in one of the 20 known PPGL predisposition genes, with mutations in the SDHx genes (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2) being the most common. The purpose of the project is to identify inhibitors of a mitochondrial transport protein, which is required for SDHB-deficient cell viability.
The goal of the project is to understand the molecular properties of this transport protein by using electron cryo-microscopy. The post-holder will participate in every stage of the process, from isolation of mitochondria, expression and purification studies, cryoEM grid preparation, data acquisition and processing, and structure model building and interpretation. Another important part will be compound screening and binding analyses to isolate tight binders for further structural analysis.
Candidates will have (or about to be awarded) a PhD in Biological or Physical Natural Sciences, and a track record of related research achievements in the area of Molecular and Structural Biology and/or Biophysics with a focus on structural biol

The Faculty of Modern and Medieval Languages and Linguistics (MMLL) at the University of Cambridge seeks to appoint a full-time permanent Assistant Professor, Associate Professor or Professor (Grade 11) in Modern Ukrainian Studies from 1 September 2027. The appointee will be a specialist in one of the following: modern Ukrainian literature, culture, cultural history, intellectual history.
The appointment may be made at any grade between Assistant Professor (Grade 9), Associate Professor (Grade 10) and Professor (Grade 11). Applications are welcome at all levels, and the eventual grade of appointment will be commensurate to the appointee's experience and standing in the field.
Candidates will have a proven record of, or clear potential for, high-quality research and a strong trajectory. Candidates will have relevant teaching experience, have successfully completed a PhD in a relevant field by the start date for the post and be able to demonstrate active, collegial engagement in research, teaching and outreach.
The appointee will contribute at undergraduate (BA) and postgraduate (MPhil and PhD) levels to the teaching and examining of Ukrainian literature, history and culture, with a particular emphasis on an introductory course on the language, literature and culture of Ukraine, which is available to all undergraduates in Modern and Medieval Languages.
They will also be expected to play an active role in supporting the academic and cultural activities of the Cambridge Ukrainian Studies programme, which seeks to deepen public understanding of Ukraine and excellent command of both Ukrainian and English is essential.

title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail:  Infrastructure system management in a changing climate
description:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at
https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/
The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance
efficiency, safety and sustainability.
Climate change and shifting patterns of extreme weather are impacting risk profiles of transport assets, requiring re-evaluation of investment strategies to maintain reliable services. This research will investigate how environmental and operational thresholds for key rail assets can be scientifically defined, quantified and integrated into long-term climate adaptation planning. The main aim of the study is to develop methods to identify tipping points arising from climatic stressors such as extreme heat, high-intensity rainfall, soil moisture variation, and compound weather events. This will require an interdisciplinary systems approach and data analysis to explore historical asset/network performance. The insight will then be used as a starting point for evaluating future performance.
This project is not about advancing fundamental physics or engineering models of a specific asset type, but rather, understanding how the data available via Network Rail can be modelled to support identification of thresholds or tipping points for the railway infrastructure system. title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Low-carbon cements for low-risk rail infrastructure applications
description:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at
https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/
The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance
efficiency, safety and sustainability.
The extensive use of cement and concrete by Network Rail across its UK rail infrastructure combined with the high emissions associated with their manufacture, are fuelling opportunities for lower carbon alternatives. Cement-based binders are widely deployed in lower strength and/or lower risk applications in conventional rail infrastructure including ancillary applications and low-risk exposure classes. These could include concrete for walkways and kerbs, blocks and pavers, drainage channels and cable troughs, signal and fence bases, some platform components and concrete fill; and mortars and grouts for slope and subgrade stabilisation, erosion control, repairs and surface treatments.
These assets have varying manufacturing, design and performance criteria. Current standards, e.g. BS EN 197 and FLEX 350 already include a range of binary and ternary low carbon cements and alternative binders, while other low compositions are not yet covered. Poor workability, limited durability data and lack of a clear acceptance route are barriers to uptake. Lower risk assets enable tailored binders, including those using recycled railway, and other secondary materials, to be assessed.
A subset will be investigated based on initial mapping of cementitious binders and applications

title: EPSRC FIBE3 CDT PhD studentship with Network Rail: Understanding rainfall-induced slope failure risk
description:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at
https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/
The project is funded in collaboration with Network Rail, the entity responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Great Britain's railway infrastructure, with an extensive network spanning thousands of miles and its complex web of tracks, stations, signalling systems and more, and is fully committed to advancing research and innovation in the field of infrastructure and built environment to enhance
efficiency, safety and sustainability.
Network Rail manage the UK's rail assets including many embankments and cuttings and possess a large amount of data from a variety of sources on their condition and performance. Failures of these slopes have a substantial impact on the rail network in terms of both safety and economic losses from speed restrictions and an understanding of the factors influencing the risk of failure is hence critical to focus remediation work on key locations within the network.
The project will aim to understand from available databases and modelling what processes and conditions drive the hotspots of failures seen around the rail network. These factors may include local geology and hydrogeologic conditions both from natural topology and the performance of drainage systems. As many of these failures are driven by periods of high rainfall, the effects of climate change on changing risks to the network will also be investigated. The project will use Network Rail data to identify common factors amongst clusters of slope failures and will then use Centrifuge and Finite Element modelling to investigate why these factors are critical and the influence of future climate changes on risk. This understanding will then allow machine learning or AI models to be used to identify risk hotspots

description:
We are seeking a Laboratory and Field Senior Technician (LFST) who will be a member of the Conservation Palaeoecology Lab (CPL) at the Department of Geography. Their work will primarily involve processing and analysing sedimentary charcoal records using the Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy to reconstruct palaeofire, data analysis and occasional field activities.
The Geography Department's laboratory and field equipment facilities, including the paleoecology lab, are at the heart of undergraduate and MPhil physical geography teaching and research. Dr Adeleye's UKRI project "Integrating past and present ecologies, and traditional knowledge for effective biodiversity management into the future (IPPET)" will inform the use of integrative palaeoecology for conservation and management. The LFST will be a vital part of the international wetland conservation palaeoecology project, which will help contextualise palaeoecological data to on-ground management needs.
Furthermore, the LFST will generate and analyse FTIR spectra data and contribute to the interpretation for research publication. They will undertake relevant training, under the guidance of the Geography Science Laboratories Manager, to maintain their skills as techniques and technologies needed to support the Department's research and teaching foci evolve.
They will also ensure spaces and equipment are well maintained and readily accessible to maximise research productivity. They will work closely with the existing CPL senior lab technician to proactively maintain laboratory and field equipment of the CPL, including stocking appropriate consumable items and ensuring the laboratories are a safe working environment for all.
The successful candidate will have experience using an FTIR machine and the application to palaeofire reconstruction, including spectra data handling, analysis and interpretation. Experience of process of plant materials for the development of FTIR spectra reference library, as well

title: PhD Studentship in Archaeobotany of the Zambezi Valley
description:
We invite applications for a 3-year funded PhD studentship starting in April 2027 under the co-supervision of Dr Alexander Weide and Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones as part of the
ZAMBEZI
project. This PhD studentship is funded as part of an ERC Advanced Grant project.
Zambezian Entanglements in the South-Central African Iron Age (ZAMBEZI) is a 5-year project based on fieldwork in Zambia and Zimbabwe. The project centres on renewed excavations at the site of Ingombe Ilede, Zambia, and exploration of the broader region, including further sites in Zambia and northern Zimbabwe. As such, ZAMBEZI will be generating new data for some key sites through which the archaeology of this region is known, and offers the opportunity to rethink second-millennium lifeways and connections in this place. The project is a collaboration with the National Museum of Zambia.
We are looking for a highly motivated applicant to join the project. The selected applicant will be jointly co-supervised by the PI of the project, Professor Stephanie Wynne-Jones, and Dr Alexander Weide, with additional input from other members of the Department and McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, and external researchers depending on training needs.
The successful applicant's research will focus on plant use, agricultural practice and landscape change, using data from flotation of material from excavations at Ingombe Ilede and neighbouring sites.
Applicants must meet the requirement for a PhD in Archaeology (see details here:
https://www.postgraduate.study.cam.ac.uk/courses/directory/aaarpdarc
), and be familiar with the archaeology of south-central Africa.
The successful applicant will become part of the ZAMBEZI project and be based at the McDonald Institute for Archaeological Research, University of Cambridge, which also hosts a large community of researchers working on a wide range of global archaeology and heritage.

It is led by its inaugural Director Professor Michael Kenny and Professor Diane Coyle, the Bennett Professor of Public Policy.
The Bennett School of Public Policy is seeking a Research Assistant/Research Associate to deliver a 12-month project on the depreciation of data assets. The 2025 System of National Accounts explicitly recognized the need to account for data as an intangible asset. This project contributes to the development of an operational framework for measuring data as an asset in the UK National Accounts. Building on ONS's experimental estimates of data investment using the sum-of-costs approach, the project will develop empirical estimates of data depreciation rates for capital stock calculations. The project will also assess the valuation methodology with a view to identifying quality measures, to better capture data's exchange value as AI use increases across the economy.
This position offers an excellent opportunity for a researcher with a strong background in econometrics and familiarity with accessing UK data from the Office for National Statistics including the Secure Research Service. Applications from candidates with backgrounds in public policy, and with experience of engaging with external audiences, including policy-makers, are particularly welcome.

We are seeking a talented and creative postdoctoral researcher to work in the Cambridge Centre for Gallium Nitride, performing growth of nitride materials and devices for applications in power electronics and characterising the resulting materials. The Cambridge Centre for Gallium Nitride is part of the Department of Materials Science and Metallurgy at the University of Cambridge and also leads the nitride activity within the EPSRC National Epitaxy Facility.

The project team also includes the capability for growth by molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), and the successful candidate will exhibit enthusiasm for collaboration across the two growth technologies to achieve optimised materials. The role may also present the opportunity for basic device fabrication to facilitate epitaxy characterisation, and hence experience of device fabrication is desirable.

title: REF Administrator (UoA12)
location_text: Office of the School of Technology
description:
Would you like to spend your time working alongside academics, supporting them with a national exercise that comes round only once every seven years?
The Research Excellence Framework decides how research funding is distributed across UK universities and how their research is judged nationally. Its results shape funding and reputation for years afterwards. The next exercise, REF2029, is submitted in November 2028.
The School of Technology is looking for a REF Administrator to support the submission for the Unit of Assessment (UoA) 12 in Engineering, the University's second largest Unit of Assessment. This UoA covers three departments in the University: Engineering; Chemical Engineering & Biotechnology; Materials Science & Metallurgy. It comprises around 260 full time equivalent research staff and expects to submit in the region of 650 research outputs, together with a portfolio of impact case studies and a Strategy, People and Research Environment (SPRE) statement.
At its heart this is a role about supporting people. REF requirements are detailed, they change as national guidance develops, and they land on academics who are already busy. You will spend much of each week in the departments rather than at a single desk, explaining what is needed in plain terms, helping researchers get their work into the system correctly, answering the questions nobody else can answer, and taking as much of the administrative load off academic colleagues as you can.
Reporting to the School REF Project Manager, you will take day to day responsibility for agreed parts of the submission, which may span research outputs, impact case studies, the SPRE statement, staff eligibility and the staff volume measure. Project description
The project, entitled
Physics-Guided Representation Learning from Free Energy Perturbation Data for Affinity Prediction and Candidate Down-Selection

Free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations provide valuable information about how strongly candidate drug molecules bind to their biological targets, but these calculations are computationally expensive. This project will investigate how machine-learning models can extract richer information from FEP data and experimental measurements, combining physical principles with modern representation-learning techniques.
The research will involve developing and evaluating new statistical and machine-learning methods, with access to both public benchmark datasets and AstraZeneca's industrial drug-discovery expertise and data.

title: Psychology of Unethical Decisions and Public Trust (Fixed Term)
description:
The Cambridge ESRC Doctoral Training Partnership [CAM-DTP] is pleased to offer an knowledge exchange studentship available for admission in October 2027.
The studentship will be co-supervised by Dr Jon Roozenbeek (Department of Psychology), Dr Lee de Wit (Department of Psychology) and Moira Nicolson (UK Cabinet Office)
Project description: 
Unethical decision-making is as a major societal problem. For instance, the Grenfell and Hillsborough disasters in the UK were preceded by a chain of decision failures. While there is some literature on how and why people make unethical decisions, why people tolerate or even reward those who do is understudied. This cross-cultural project will explore the psychology of unethical decision-making: what drives it, and how the public perceives it, and its connection to trust in public and private institutions.
ESRC Research Priority Areas: Security, risk and resilience, Understanding behaviour.
Research skills you must have if applying for this topic:
Understanding of survey research, randomised controlled trials, and longitudinal (cohort) studies
Ability to work with longitudinal "big datasets", e.g., social media data, both in terms of collection and analysis
Research skills it would be helpful to have if applying for this topic:
Knowledge of governmental accountability frameworks (especially in the UK)
Knowledge of politics in non-Western contexts (e.g., India, China, Russia)
Familiarity with multiple languages

University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh, Imperial College London and University of Oxford.
Applications are invited for 10 funded 4-year PhD studentships starting in October 2027, as part of the British Heart Foundation (BHF) doctoral training programme focused on preventing cardiovascular disease through innovative, data-driven approaches.
This interdisciplinary PhD programme brings together leading researchers from the University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh, Imperial College London, and the University of Oxford. Students will be trained to work at the intersection of population health, systems biology, and data science/AI, combining expertise across these fields to tackle one of the most pressing challenges in global health. Students will be based in one of the following institutes:  Cambridge (5 studentships), Edinburgh (2 studentships), Imperial (1 Studentship) or Oxford (2 studentships) while benefiting from training, co-supervision, and collaboration across the partner institutions. Projects will span a range of topics including health data science, AI and machine learning, multi-omics, epidemiology, and translational cardiovascular research. Students will be part of a cohort-based programme, gaining access to shared training activities, collaborative networks, and state-of-the-art data resources across the multi-institute partnership.
This four-year PhD programme combines interdisciplinary training with in-depth research. From world-renowned and loved museums to nationally significant historic buildings, industrial heritage sites and collections stores, our estate is central to everything we do. User Researcher
We care for millions of public records spanning government, courts and parliament. Our oldest records are from over a thousand years ago. We are committed to making these collections accessible through high-quality digital services for future generations.
As a User Researcher, you will help teams understand user needs and behaviours through evidence-based research. Using a range of qualitative and quantitative research methods, you will generate insights that inform service design, support decision-making and ensure our products and services meet the needs of diverse users. You will work closely with multidisciplinary teams to identify opportunities, shape solutions and advocate for users throughout the product lifecycle.
This is a unique opportunity to undertake user research in an environment focused on complex information services rather than purely transactional services. You will work alongside experts from across our collections and research communities while contributing to the future access of public records through our digital services.
This role would suit someone who is curious, analytical and motivated by solving complex problems through research and evidence.
You will enjoy working collaboratively in multidisciplinary teams, communicating insights to a range of audiences and helping teams make better decisions based on user needs. You will be comfortable balancing short-term delivery priorities with the development of longer-term organisational understanding of users and their behaviours.

Governance Manager - Annual Reporting and Transparency
Based within the Chief Executive’s Office, the Governance Manager – Annual Reporting and Transparency (‘the Governance Manager’) will deliver a range of activities to support The National Archives’ corporate governance function and the Keeper’s statutory responsibilities, providing dedicated lead professional secretariat support as needed.
Specifically, the Governance Manager will lead the project management of The National Archives’ Annual report and accounts. This involves coordinating with senior stakeholders both internally and externally including the Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) and Treasury to ensure that the document meets statutory requirements and is laid before Parliament in a timely manner. The Governance Manager will coordinate the work to fulfil The National Archives’ wider obligations around Transparency
The Governance Manager will also provide secretariat support to The National Archives Board’s subcommittees – the Finance and Performance Committee and the Audit and Risk Committee and other meetings and committees as required.
The Governance Manager - Annual Reporting and Transparency will work alongside the Governance Manager – Secretary to The National Archives Board and the Advisory Council, to ensure that the Board and its subcommittees receive high-quality and coordinated support and with the Head of Chief Executive’s Office to ensure that The National Archives’ corporate governance continues to meet the standards set by Government.

Governance Manager - Secretary to The National Archives’ Board and the Advisory Council
Based within the Chief Executive’s Office, the Governance Manager - Secretary to The National Archives Board and the Advisory Council on National Records and Archives (‘the Secretary’) provides dedicated lead professional secretariat support to The National Archives Board and to the independent Advisory Council on National Records and Archives (ACNRA), and its subcommittees, The Forum on Historical Manuscripts and Academic Research and provide support with The Manorial and Tithe Documents Panel. More broadly, the Secretary delivers a range of activities to support The National Archives’ corporate governance function and the Keeper’s statutory responsibilities.
The National Archives’ Board (the Board) is the key strategic advisory body of The National Archives. and is responsible for ensuring that the leadership of The National Archives sets the strategic direction and makes strategic choices; provides leadership in the delivery of statutory, corporate and business responsibilities; makes key investment, procurement and project decisions that withstand scrutiny; identifies and manages risks effectively; encourages improvements in performance across the organisation; and takes corporate responsibility for its decisions and their implementation.
The Advisory Council is chaired by the Master of the Rolls and is an advisory non-departmental public body reporting to the Secretary of State for the Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). Head of Digital Products and Experience
Can you shape the digital transformation of one of the UK's most visited museum groups?
About us
The Science Museum Group (SMG) is a world-leading cultural organisation, welcoming millions of visitors each year to the Science Museum in London, the Science and Industry Museum in Manchester, the National Railway Museum in York, Locomotion in Shildon, and the National Science and Media Museum in Bradford.
Digital is changing how people discover culture, plan visits and connect with meaningful stories. At SMG, this creates an exciting opportunity to make our collections more accessible, relevant and engaging through audience-first digital experiences.
Over the next four years, we will bring our websites, online collections and museum experiences together into a more seamless digital journey, expanding our reach, boosting commercial resilience and building the skills and responsible AI practices needed to innovate with confidence.
We are seeking a Head of Digital Products and Experience to develop SMG's goal for a more connected digital experience across our sites. This is a full-time role (35 hours per week) and can be based at any Science Museum Group site.
The role currently works to a hybrid working pattern, which offers flexibility to work from home. There will be a requirement to travel between our sites with frequent travel to London as this is where a majority of the team sit.

Schools Learning Producer
About us
Royal Museums Greenwich is a collection of diverse historical sites. The sites are the National Maritime Museum, Cutty Sark, the Royal Observatory, and the Queen’s House. Each of these sites has a unique identity and a common purpose to serve our communities, through sharing our collections and expertise. We are a place to explore the sea, space, art and history, and our strategy ‘Charting Our Course’ puts people at the core of its success.
The Role
If you are passionate about the role Museums play in the learning journeys of children and young people, then this is the role for you. We are looking for a dynamic individual to work with schools and teachers to support and inspire collections-based learning at the National Maritime Museum and the Queen’s House. You will lead on the development, delivery and resourcing of historical enquiry programmes from early years to post 16, giving all school learners a high-quality experience that is unique to our sites. You will also nurture relationships with key internal and external stakeholders, ensuring that audience voice is embedded into everything we do.
The successful candidate will have a proven track record of engaging children and young people using museum collections and a great understanding of the needs of school learners and teachers. Effective time management and written and verbal presentation skills are also required. This role involves working with histories relating to empire and the transatlantic trade of enslaved people so experience of culturally sensitive approaches to exploring these topics is essential. It’s a fast-paced and rewarding role that puts learning at the centre of the Museum.
